--- title: "Buying a Home, Measured in Hours of Work" subtitle: "The monthly payment takes fewer hours than it did in 1990. The hard part now is getting in the door." author: "SixtyEight95" date: "2026-11-12" categories: [housing, cost of living, wages] image: infographic.png --- ::: {.cell} ::: "Nobody can afford a house anymore" might be the most repeated money complaint in America. We wanted to know how true it is, so we measured the cost of a home the way it actually feels: **in hours of work.** ## The short answer ::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"} The mortgage on a typical new home takes about **71 hours of work a month** today. That's a lot more than in 2021 (56 hours), but **less than in 1990** (96 hours). The monthly payment isn't the worst it's ever been. **The down payment is the bigger wall.** ::: ## What "hours of work" means We take the monthly mortgage payment on a median-priced new home and divide it by what the average worker earns per hour, before taxes. The answer is how many hours of work it takes to cover the payment each month. For scale: a full-time job is about **173 hours a month.** So today's 71 hours is roughly 41% of one person's pay before taxes. (Many households have two earners, which makes it easier, but we stick to one so the comparison is the same in every year.) ## 50 years of mortgage payments, in hours ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: Hover to see the price, the rate, and the payment behind each point. The worst moment was the end of **1981**, when mortgage rates were near **18%** and the payment took **124 hours** a month. The best was **2011**, at **49 hours**, with rates around 4%. ## Interest rates are the big lever Notice what happened between 2021 and 2023. Home prices relative to pay barely moved, but the payment went from 56 hours to 87 hours of work a month. That jump was almost all interest rates, which went from about 3% to 6.8%. To see how much rates matter: today's median new home costs about **$406,900**. At today's rate (about 6.4%), the monthly payment is about **$2,280**. At 2021's rate, the same house would cost **$1,536** a month. Same house, **$744 a month** difference. ## The catch: getting in the door The monthly payment is only half the story. Before you get a mortgage, you need a down payment, and that depends on the price of the house, not the interest rate. ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: A 10% down payment on a typical new home is about **$40,690** today. That's **7.3 months of the average worker's full pay**, before taxes and before spending a dime on anything else. In 1985 it was 5.6 months. That's why buying feels so out of reach even though the monthly payment isn't at a record: the house itself costs more years of pay than it did in the 1980s, so the savings hurdle is higher. ## Snapshot by year ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} |Year | Median new home| Mortgage rate| Monthly payment| Hours of work / month| 10% down, in months of pay| |:-------------|---------------:|-------------:|---------------:|---------------------:|--------------------------:| |1975 | $39,275| 9%| $286| 60| 4.8| |1981 | $68,950| 16.6%| $867| 116| 5.4| |1985 | $84,275| 12.4%| $805| 92| 5.6| |1990 | $122,300| 10.1%| $977| 96| 6.9| |2000 | $167,550| 8.1%| $1,112| 79| 6.9| |2006 | $243,750| 6.4%| $1,374| 82| 8.4| |2012 | $244,400| 3.7%| $1,007| 51| 7.2| |2019 | $320,250| 3.9%| $1,365| 58| 7.9| |2021 | $383,000| 3%| $1,446| 56| 8.5| |2023 | $426,525| 6.8%| $2,505| 87| 8.5| |2026 (so far) | $405,100| 6.4%| $2,280| 71| 7.3| ::: ::: ## The fine print - **Principal and interest only.** Property taxes and homeowners insurance aren't included, and insurance in particular has gotten much more expensive in many states. Real monthly costs are higher than shown. - **Newly built homes.** The government's long-running median price series covers new homes. Existing homes follow a similar trend, but prices differ. - **National medians.** A typical home in San Francisco and one in Toledo are very different stories. - **One average earner, before taxes.** Your own hours depend on your pay and your household. ## The bottom line Monthly mortgage payments are high compared with the cheap-money years of 2010–2021, but not compared with the 1980s and early '90s. What's genuinely harder now is the price of entry: the down payment takes more of a paycheck than it did a generation ago. If rates come down, the monthly payment gets easier fast. The down payment problem only gets easier if pay grows faster than home prices. --- **How we did this.** Home prices are the median sales price of new houses sold in the U.S. (Census Bureau and HUD). Mortgage rates are Freddie Mac's 30-year fixed average. Pay is average hourly earnings of production and nonsupervisory employees (about 80% of private-sector workers) from the Bureau of Labor Statistics. All series come from [FRED](https://fred.stlouisfed.org/). We assume 10% down and a 30-year fixed loan at that quarter's average rate. Hours of work = monthly payment ÷ hourly pay. "Today" is the average of the latest four quarters (through Q3 2026).
